The Rolex Daytona was first introduced in 1963 and over the decades of fine tuning and upgrades, it became one of Rolex's most famous and sought after models due to its role in popular culture and watch collecting. The reference 5513, introduced circa 1962, offered a more accessible alternative to the chronometer-certified 5512, sharing its design and attributes while featuring a non-chronometer movement. Rather than replacing the 5512, the 5513 was sold alongside it, quickly becoming a cornerstone of the Submariner line.

Produced from the mid-1960s, Meters First dials overlapped with Feet First dials between late 1968 and early 1970, likely reflecting RolexÃ¢ÂÂs efforts to appeal to the U.S. market, which did not widely use the metric system.
Distinctive features of this dial include semi-open 6Ã¢ÂÂs in the depth rating and the characteristic straight-top Ã¢ÂÂSÃ¢ÂÂ in Ã¢ÂÂSubmariner.Ã¢ÂÂ

The reference 1680 was introduced in the late 1960s and remained in production until 1980, with the Red Submariner standing today as one of the most coveted iterations within the Submariner family.
Produced from approximately 1967 to 1975, early examples of the reference 1680 are distinguished by the Ã¢ÂÂSubmarinerÃ¢ÂÂ designation printed in red on the dial rather than the standard white, a detail that has become emblematic of the modelÃ¢ÂÂs appeal among collectors.
The reference 1680 is historically significant as the first Submariner to feature a date complication, paired with RolexÃ¢ÂÂs Cyclops magnification lens. The crystal was also modified for this reference, rising approximately 3 mm above the case and bezel, further setting it apart from earlier Submariner models.
Seven distinct dial variants were produced for the Red Submariner 1680. The present example is fitted with a Mark IV dial, representing the earliest Feet First configuration. The watchÃ¢ÂÂs vintage character is further enhanced by evenly aged luminous material, underscoring the utilitarian aesthetic that defines the Submariner. Remarkably, for a watch now more than half a century old, the overall condition remains notably well preserved.

The Rolex Sea-Dweller was first introduced in 1967 as a more robust answer to the Submariner.Â Featuring a pioneering, yet-to-be patented helium escape valve, the new model could accompany divers to extreme depths of 610 meters.Â The valve allows helium and other gases to escape, enabling the watch to withstand compression during saturation diving and preventing the acrylic crystal from popping out on the ascent to the surface.Â On the dial, two lines of text were printed in red: The Sea-Dweller text, and below, Submariner 2000, thus giving the watch its nick name, the Ã¢ÂÂDouble Red.Ã¢ÂÂÂ While retaining the SubmarinerÃ¢ÂÂs date window at 3 oÃ¢ÂÂclock, it notably omitted the cyclops lens over the plexiglass.
The current example features an attractive, late version of the Mark IV dial.Â The case was gently polished when it was serviced approximately 40 years ago and retains its original contours.

Manufactured from 2001 until 2008, the Ref. 5134 continued Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs line of Travel Time watches well into the new century. True to previous Travel Time references, such as the predecessor Ref. 5034, the 5134 retained a version of the 215 PS caliber, a manually wound movement that controlled a 24-hour sub-dial for the second time zone, as well as sub-seconds.Â 
The dual time feature on this watch is kept by an extra hour hand that can be hidden underneath the primary one when it is not in use. This hand is triggered by the two pushers on the left side of the case.

In the spring of 1996, Patek Philippe introduced a timepiece that would soon redefine modern calendar complications. That same autumn, the model was awarded Ã¢ÂÂWatch of the YearÃ¢ÂÂ by the Swiss magazine Montres Passion, at a time when such distinctions were still rare.
The innovation lay in its practicality. Positioned between the traditional calendar, which requires adjustment five times per year for months shorter than 31 days, and the perpetual calendar, which requires no correction but is considerably more complex and costly, the Annual Calendar offered an elegant solution. Its ingenious mechanism required adjustment only once per year, at the end of February.
While Patek Philippe has never claimed to have invented the Annual Calendar outright, there was nothing comparable on the market when its design and engineering department began development in the early 1990s. The result was a patented and profoundly original mechanism, introduced in 1996 as reference 5035. Housed in a 37 mm case and powered by the caliber 315 S QA 24H, the model was distinguished by its balanced dial layout and applied Roman numerals.
Building on the success of the reference 5035, Patek Philippe expanded the line with numerous iterations, including in the introduction of reference 5146 in 2006. The present example belongs to this later generation, featuring a 39 mm case and, in bracelet configuration, elegant gold drop-link construction paired with a cream dial and applied gold hour markers. Bracelet versions were produced in yellow, white, and rose gold.
The present example offers the opportunity to acquire a timepiece featuring one of Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs most enduring and commercially successful complications of the past three decades.

At the beginning of the 1960s, Patek Philippe ceased production of chronographs, while remaining fully committed to the development of complicated watches with self-winding movements. It was not until the mid-1980s that the firm reintroduced the perpetual calendar chronograph with the Reference 3970, the direct descendant of the celebrated Reference 2499 of the 1950s and Reference 1518 of the 1940s.

Caliber CH 27-70 QThe Reference 2499 was produced in four distinct series, concluding its remarkable production run in 1985, when Patek Philippe exhausted its supply of the classic hand-wound Valjoux 23 VZ. Thereafter, the manufacture secured an exclusive version of the Nouvelle Lemania 27-70 caliber, successor to the Valjoux movement. Originally introduced in 1968, this caliber would later beat at the heart of the Reference 3970.
Nouvelle Lemania, a privately owned family company renowned for its high-quality chronograph movements, willingly modified and adapted its ÃÂ©bauches to meet Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs exacting standards. In Geneva, exclusivity required extensive reworking: nearly all components were revised, while finishing, assembly, regulation, and inspection were performed entirely in-house.
The Ã¢ÂÂThird SeriesÃ¢ÂÂOver the course of the Reference 3970Ã¢ÂÂs production, the model evolved through four clearly defined series, each distinguished by subtle variations in dial design, typography, and aesthetics.
The present example belongs to the third series. Watches of this series were delivered with a solid screw-down case back, accompanied by an additional sapphire crystal case back. Leaf hands were replaced with baton hands, and the hour markers became pointed and faceted to harmonize with the revised handset. According to Tortella, 93 pieces have been identified within the distribution of yellow gold cases.
The dial is notably brighter in appearance, and in most third-series examples, the calendar discs feature a sans-serif font, lending a more contemporary character compared to earlier executions.

The archives and special collections held by General Motors document the centuries long history of GM as a corporation and as a cultural entity. 
In addition to documents and literature, the archives also house a global archive of historical photography, motion picture film, video and digital media. The archive was established in 1993 and built on the foundations laid by the GM Photographic division which dates to 1920. 
GM Photographic was created to document the development, manufacturing and promotion of General Motors products as well as its events, facilities and leadership. The millions of photographic images and hours of motion picture footage comprises a significate portion of GM's archives and special collections today with more than 8 million photographic images, 220,000 video masters, 25,000 motion picture films and 1.5 million digital media files.
The present Reference 96 features a charming engraving on the case back of 'GM Photographic' for a Mr. 'Richard B. Collick 1930-1955' likely commemorating Mr. Collick's tenure at the firm.

Introduced during a period when Patek Philippe emphasized both aesthetical and technical refinement, the reference 2509 was notable for its robust waterproof case crafted by Taubert & Fils, marked by Geneva Key 11 on the inside case back, a notable maker that spearheaded modern case making and that was famous for their screw down case back designs.

The Tourbillon Souverain from F.P. Journe is his signature model, known for its groundbreaking and award-winning use of theÂ remontoir d'ÃÂgalitÃÂ©. Launched in 1999, it became the first tourbillon wristwatch to incorporate these dual complications. In 2019, F.P. Journe commemorated the 20th anniversary of his tourbillon movement by introducing the Tourbillon Souverain Vertical. This redesign hinges on a fundamental improvement: rotating the tourbillon cage 90 degrees from the standard configuration to counteract gravitational effects on the balance wheel, even when the watch lies flat. In traditional configurations, a tourbillon positioned parallel to the dial is ineffective when the watch is flat since gravityÃ¢ÂÂs pull is perpendicular to the rotating cage. However, with this vertical orientation, the Tourbillon Souverain Vertical remains responsive to gravitational disturbances in nearly any position. In his own words, Ã¢ÂÂI designed this vertical tourbillon so that the tourbillonÃ¢ÂÂs functions remain constant whether the watch lies flat or is placed on its side, and the amplitude is subsequently the same, whether with a deployant clasp lying on the side or with an ardillon buckle lying flat.Ã¢ÂÂ
